notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 7, drawn from the pages actually read. I have noted the source for each point. The chapter is a climactic prophecy of doom: "the end" has come upon the whole land; judgment is certain, imminent, and without pity.

---

## Overview

- **Ellicott**: The prophecy is "occupied with the nearness and the completeness of the judgment already foretold. It takes the form, to some extent, of a song of lamentation; and is more thoroughly poetic in its structure than anything which has gone before." The repetitions are designed and give force to the denunciation. Ellicott notes this chapter closes the first series of Ezekiel's prophecies (Ezek 4–7), all uttered within about a year and two months of his call. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/7.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch**: The chapter "completes the announcement of judgment upon Jerusalem and Judah, by expanding the thought, that the end will come both quickly and inevitably upon the land and people." Verses 1–4 give the theme; vv. 5–27 are arranged in four strophes. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-7.html)
- **Constable (Evangelical)**: Six parts to this summary message: (1) God's determination to bring judgment, vv. 1–4; (2) the repeated call for judgment, vv. 5–9; (3) imminence and certainty, vv. 10–13; (4) total destruction, vv. 14–18; (5) uselessness of physical resources, vv. 19–22; (6) the fall of Jerusalem, vv. 23–27. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-7.html)
- **Calvin**: The repetitions are deliberate. "If God had only uttered his commands shortly, when the people were not only slow to believe but of a perverse disposition, his message had proved cold and ineffectual." The phrase "an end" is emphatically repeated to break through Israel's false hope that God could always be appeased. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-7.html)

---

## v. 1 — "And the word of the LORD came to me, saying,"

- **Guzik**: This phrase reminds us Ezekiel was fundamentally a prophet — a man to whom the word of the LORD came and who then had to deliver it. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: The phrase "word of the LORD came" occurs 49x in Ezekiel. The chapter is filled with short, staccato-like phrases emphasising the imminence of destruction. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_71-13)
- **Calvin**: "The word was given by Jehovah" — the prophecy is distinguished from the former; God sent Ezekiel twice so the people would understand "that not once only, but twice and perpetually, what he heard from God's mouth was to be repeated." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-7.html)

---

## v. 2 — "O son of man, this is what the Lord GOD says to the land of Israel: 'The end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land.'"

- **Guzik**: Ezekiel was in Babylon, yet this message was "to the land of Israel" — Jerusalem had not yet been destroyed. "Four corners" means no place would be spared. Morgan says, "The words here 'An end' are exclamatory. That is the message in its entirety — 'An end!' The time of patience was over, there was to be no more waiting." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: The Hebrew word for "end" (qets) is related to ripe summer fruit ready to be harvested (Amos 8:1-3). Harvesting means cutting down and clearing the fields. The Hebrew verb "coming" is in the perfect tense, expressing certainty. Matthew Henry: "When the town is on fire men do not seek for fine words … the prophet here proclaims, An end! an end! … He that hath ears to hear let him hear." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_71-13)
- **Calvin**: "An end is coming, an end upon the four corners of the land." God had already inflicted moderate punishments; the people thought themselves escaped. The word "end" reproves their obstinacy: "God had displayed a remarkable specimen of clemency in punishing the Israelites so lightly when he might utterly have cut them off." Now the end has truly come. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-7.html)
- **Constable**: The Lord announced that He was bringing an end on the whole land; it was coming soon. The recurrence of identical words emphasises the certainty, extent, and basis of coming judgment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-7.html)

---

## v. 3 — "The end is now upon you, and I will unleash My anger against you. I will judge you according to your ways and repay you for all your abominations."

- **Gill**: The repetition is for confirmation and application — God speaks now in the second person to arouse attention. "I will send mine anger upon thee" means the token of His anger, the punishment of sins. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/7.htm)
- **Precept Austin**: "I will send (shalach) My anger" pictures God's arrows of judgment released from His bow. The Hebrew word for anger (aph) literally means "nose" — evoking the image of nostrils flaring in passionate wrath. "Abominations" (toebah) refers to what is detestable, loathsome, disgusting — especially idolatry. "Judah's own vile standard would be used to condemn her." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_71-13)
- **Guzik**: God promised simple justice — "their ways would determine their judgment." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)

---

## v. 4 — "I will not look on you with pity, nor will I spare you, but I will punish you for your ways and for the abominations among you. Then you will know that I am the LORD."

- **Guzik**: The judgment would be severe — no pity, no sparing. Yet the great judgment had a good purpose: "It would be the way that God's people would return to a true relationship with, and knowledge of, their covenant God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: The "recognition formula" — "then you will know that I am the LORD" — appears three times in this chapter (vv. 4, 9, 27) and 63 times in Ezekiel. God's purpose is that He be recognised as the true God through His acts of judgment. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_723-27)
- **Matthew Henry (from search excerpt)**: "Oh that the wickedness of the wicked might end before it bring them to an end! … The day of real trouble is near, not a mere echo or rumour of troubles. Whatever are the fruits of God's judgments, our sin is the root of them." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/7.htm)

---

## v. 5 — "This is what the Lord GOD says: 'Disaster! An unprecedented disaster—behold, it is coming!'"

- **Guzik**: The short, excited phrases were spoken "as if they were in the mouth of someone watching this overwhelming army do its damage." The disaster is "singular" — unprecedented, unique in its horror. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Constable**: A unique disaster was coming — "This oracle stresses the horror and surprise of the coming judgment as well as the person judging." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-7.html)

---

## vv. 6–7 — "The end has come! The end has come! It has roused itself against you. Behold, it has come! Doom has come to you … there is panic on the mountains instead of shouts of joy."

- **Guzik**: The people would face a dawn, but a "dawn of doom." The "rejoicing in the mountains" refers to pagan altars and perverted worship. Feinberg notes a "beautiful play on words" — the end is pictured "as though it had been quiescent or asleep, but would be awakened and aroused." Poole: "God's vengeance seems to slumber, and sinners dream it will never awake, but here the prophet assureth … that God hath awakened his vengeance." Morgan adds that the prophet was telling the exiles "what Jeremiah was telling them in Jerusalem, that the opportunity for recovery was past, that the nation had overstepped the boundaries of the forbearance and waiting of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Calvin**: "An end is come, an end is come: it has been watchful against thee: behold it is come." The verb "has watched" signifies haste. God had delayed, but would no longer refrain. The repetition was necessary because the people "were always supposing that God could be appeased by various means." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-7.html)

---

## vv. 8–9 — "Very soon I will pour out My wrath upon you … I will judge you according to your ways … Then you will know that it is I, the LORD, who strikes the blow."

- **Guzik**: "Abominations" mainly has the sense of disgusting idolatry. A new name for God is revealed: "YHWH makkeh" — "The Lord who strikes the blow" (Alexander). The judgment would show idols were powerless. "In destroying their reliance on idols, they could come back to a true relationship with Yahweh." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Ellicott**: In v. 4 it only says "ye shall know that I am the LORD"; here it is specified — "they shall know that God is a God of judgment, and that these calamities are from Him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/7.htm)

---

## v. 10 — "Behold, the day is here! It has come! Doom has gone out, the rod has budded, arrogance has bloomed."

- **Guzik**: "The rod has blossomed, pride has budded" is an ironic reference to Aaron's rod that budded (Num 17). That was a supernatural demonstration of God's favour; this would be a supernatural demonstration of God's anger. Block: "Ezekiel has hereby twisted what was originally a positive symbol of election and legitimate authority into an emblematic cudgel of oppression and wickedness." Alternatively, Smith identifies the rod as Babylon: "God's judgment 'rod.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Dummelow**: The meaning is "rather obscure." If the rod is chastisement, pride means the same. "Babylon is called 'Pride' in Jeremiah 50:31." Alternatively, the violence in v. 11 seems to be Israel's, and "the rod of wickedness" a figure for its developed form. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-7.html)

---

## v. 11 — "Their violence has grown into a rod to punish their wickedness. None of them will remain: none of their multitude, none of their wealth, and nothing of value."

- **Guzik**: With poetic power and repetition ("none… none… none"), Ezekiel assured them none would escape. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Layman's Bible Commentary**: "The ultimate consequences of national character have come to full bloom. Violent strength and the power of wealth are useless. Among people in siege or captivity, there is no pre-eminence." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/ezekiel-7.html)

---

## vv. 12–13 — "Let the buyer not rejoice and the seller not mourn … The seller will surely not recover what he sold while both remain alive. For the vision concerning the whole multitude will not be revoked …"

- **Guzik**: Both buyer and seller would have reason to mourn — buying and selling lose significance in total disaster. "In a grim parody of the ancient laws of Jubilee, the prophet declares that patrimonial property that has been lost to the family will not return; the year of Jubilee will be canceled" (Block). Normally, when God announces judgment it is an implied invitation for repentance, after which God relents — but here "it shall not turn back." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Constable**: "It would be impossible for sellers to regain (by redemption or in a sabbatical or jubilee year) what they sold because everything would be swept away before a change could be made (cf. 1 Corinthians 7:29-31)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-7.html)

---

## v. 14 — "They have blown the trumpet and made everything ready, but no one goes to war, for My wrath is upon the whole multitude."

- **Guzik**: There would be very little resistance to the Babylonian conquest. Morgan: "Its first manifestation would be the paralysis of the people, so that when the trumpet was blown for the battle, and all was ready, none would move forward, being overcome by terror and grief." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin** (quoting Craigie): "The spontaneous reaction to threat was to turn to that old standby, the army; that reaction, rooted in a long history of self-confidence, and lack of confidence in God, illustrated one of the reasons why judgment was coming." Not only was the Lord not for them — He was actually against them. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_714-22)

---

## v. 15 — "The sword is outside; plague and famine are within. Those in the country will die by the sword, and those in the city will be devoured by famine and plague."

- **Guzik**: Ezekiel methodically described the fate of those in the field, those in the city, and survivors. Each would experience the calamity in their own way, but none would escape. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: This echoes the curses of Deuteronomy 32:23-25 and the earlier prophecy of Ezekiel 5:12 (a third by plague, a third by sword, a third scattered). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_714-22)

---

## v. 16 — "The survivors will escape and live in the mountains, moaning like doves of the valley, each for his own iniquity."

- **Guzik**: Block explains that the prophet envisages total destruction of towns and cities, forcing survivors to the mountains, their mourning resembling "the plaintive cooing of ordinary pigeons." They mourn "each for his own iniquity" — personal, not just national, guilt. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: The mourning is over the catastrophe and resulting famine/plague, not necessarily true repentance. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_714-22)

---

## v. 17 — "Every hand will go limp, and every knee will turn to water."

- **Guzik**: Vawter and Hoppe explain "all knees weak as water" is a euphemism "for the loss of bladder control in moments of terror." The LXX translators render it "all their knees will run with urine." Block confirms: "The prophet is hereby referring to the loss of bladder control that occurs in a moment of extreme crisis." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: "Limp hands" describe complete paralysis of strength induced by overwhelming fear. "Knees will become like water" — the Greek Septuagint similarly has "all thighs shall be defiled with moisture." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_714-22)

---

## v. 18 — "They will put on sackcloth, and terror will overwhelm them. Shame will cover all their faces, and all their heads will be shaved."

- **Guzik**: The calamity would not be light — all would share in the horror and shame. Sackcloth and shaved heads are traditional signs of mourning in the ancient Near East. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: Sackcloth chafed the skin and served as a continual reminder of the pain of loss. Shuddering refers to such severe distress as to cause involuntary trembling. But these were not signs of true repentance — the people mourned the catastrophe, not their sin. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_714-22)

---

## v. 19 — "They will throw their silver into the streets, and their gold will seem unclean. Their silver and gold cannot save them … They cannot satisfy their appetites or fill their stomachs with wealth, for it became the stumbling block that brought their iniquity."

- **Guzik**: The completeness of judgment affected rich and poor alike. Silver and gold would be thrown into the streets as burdensome and useless. Trapp compares it to Judas throwing away his wages of wickedness. Meyer: "Generally silver and gold stand for much among the children of men … But when the supreme crises come … there is no help in silver and gold; they cannot satisfy or save." The word translated "refuse" (nidda) "belongs to the language of female impurity and expresses the revulsion that will be felt." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin** (quoting Cooper): "The silver and gold was worthless for averting judgment. This was a sobering reality for a materialistic society." Quoting Craigie: "It is dependence on wealth that is condemned, and the delusion of money's security that is shattered." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_714-22)

---

## v. 20 — "His beautiful ornaments they transformed into pride and used them to fashion their vile images and detestable idols. Therefore I will make these into something unclean for them."

- **Guzik**: God blessed Israel with wealth and resources, but they used those things to promote idolatry. The "beautiful ornaments" likely refer to gold and silver from the temple that were made into idols. Fittingly, all that wealth would be given as plunder to strangers. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: "Pride" is used 9x in Ezekiel. Personal jewellery once given to adorn the tabernacle and temple was used to beautify pagan shrines. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_714-22)
- **Constable**: "The people had become proud over the glorious splendor of Jerusalem and the temple and, as the height of arrogance, had used some of the temple treasures to make idols." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-7.html)

---

## vv. 21–22 — "I will hand these things over as plunder to foreigners and loot to the wicked of the earth, who will defile them. I will turn My face away from them, and they will defile My treasured place. Violent men will enter it, and they will defile it."

- **Guzik**: God would give Israel's wealth to foreigners. He even announced robbers would sack His temple, including the "secret place" (the Holy of Holies). The judgment would be complete, not sparing even the temple. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: "I will also turn My face from them" — this would be incredible to the exiles because Jehovah had chosen Jerusalem as His dwelling and had miraculously fought for the city in the past. Judah had come to accept the notion the city could not be touched by pagan nations. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_714-22)

---

## v. 23 — "Forge the chain, for the land is full of crimes of bloodshed, and the city is full of violence."

- **Guzik**: This was likely a chain to restrain violent criminals. Feinberg says Ezekiel was commanded to perform a symbolic act — "making a chain which was emblematic of the captivity awaiting them (see Jeremiah 27:2; Nahum 3:10)." Block notes "this word describes the treatment of prisoners of war … the 'chain' would have been used to tie the captives together to form a long train headed for exile." "Crimes of blood" (only here) is best understood as "murderous judicial decisions." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: "Make the chain" is a command — a sign act. "Judah had sown violence and bloodshed and was now reaping this captivity as its harvest. God's law of reaping and sowing is sure." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_723-27)

---

## v. 24 — "So I will bring the most wicked of nations to take possession of their houses. I will end the pride of the mighty, and their holy places will be profaned."

- **Guzik**: God made no claim the invaders would be righteous — they were "the worst of the Gentiles" (the Babylonians/Chaldeans). Trapp: "The Jews were bad enough, but the Chaldees were worse, if worse might be; malignants above measure … A hard knot must have a harder wedge." Block: "How he may use a more wicked population to punish a less wicked one may create theological problems for mortal minds, but it is consistent with his sovereignty over all." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: "Their holy places will be profaned" — what irony: God will profane places "which were holy to men but not holy to Him! What men call religion is often a stench in God's nostrils!" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_723-27)

---

## v. 25 — "Anguish is coming! They will seek peace, but find none."

- **Guzik**: There would be no quickly made peace treaty or tribute to prevent the disaster. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: "The divine formula is simple — Know God, know peace! No God, no peace!" Quoting Isaiah 57:21: "There is no peace," says my God, "for the wicked." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_723-27)

---

## v. 26 — "Disaster upon disaster will come, and rumor after rumor. Then they will seek a vision from a prophet, but instruction from the priests will perish, as will counsel from the elders."

- **Guzik**: This seems to be a direct answer to what was said in Jerusalem, as recorded in Jeremiah 18:18 — where the people boasted "the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet." God answers: yes, they will. In the day of judgment, frightened people will finally seek a word from God — but there will be none. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Ellicott**: "The three chief sources of counsel, the prophets, the priests, and the elders, are all represented as applied to in vain. God had forsaken the people who had rejected Him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/7.htm)
- **Precept Austin**: Echoes Amos 8:11-12 — a famine "for hearing the words of the LORD." People will go to and fro to seek it but not find it. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_723-27)
- **Layman's Bible Commentary**: "Ordinary sources of strength in any society break down under pressure in Judah … Prophetic vision, priestly interpretation, elders' advice, and royal leadership all fail." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/ezekiel-7.html)

---

## v. 27 — "The king will mourn, the prince will be clothed with despair, and the hands of the people of the land will tremble. I will deal with them according to their conduct, and I will judge them by their own standards. Then they will know that I am the LORD."

- **Guzik**: Wiersbe notes that in Ezekiel's eyes, the king was Jehoiachin (Ezek 1:2) and the prince was Zedekiah. Though Zedekiah was the last king, the prophet didn't recognise his reign and considered him only a prince (cf. Ezek 12:10, 12). The judgment would be terrible because Israel had sinned greatly, yet the triple repetition of "then they shall know that I am the LORD" shows God's purpose was not pain but restoration. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)
- **Precept Austin**: "According to their conduct I will deal with them, and by their judgments I will judge them" — God judged Israel by her own standards, the Mosaic covenant they should have known and followed. Matthew 7:2: "For in the way you judge, you will be judged." The recognition formula closes the chapter: by judging Judah according to the standards declared in the Mosaic covenant, the Lord would cause them to recognise Him as different from the gods of the nations — "a God not to be manipulated or taken for granted, but rather obeyed and trusted wholeheartedly." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_723-27)

---

## Traditional Differences Among Protestant Traditions

The sources searched show broad agreement on the plain meaning of Ezekiel 7. No sharp denominational disputes emerged from the sites consulted. However, some distinct emphases are visible:

- **Reformed (Calvin)**: Emphasises God's sovereignty and the deliberate pedagogy of repetition. Calvin stresses that God used moderate chastisements first, and the "end" only came after Israel proved incorrigible. The repetitions were necessary because of human obstinacy. The use of a more wicked nation (Babylon) to punish a less wicked one "may create theological problems for mortal minds, but it is consistent with his sovereignty over all" (Block, quoted by Guzik). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-7.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-7/)

- **Dispensational / Pre-millennial (Precept Austin / MacArthur / Wiersbe)**: Precept Austin explicitly states a "literal interpretation … a belief that God is not yet finished with the nation of Israel, a belief in a literal return of Christ to literally reign and rule on the earth for 1000 years." The commentary draws application from Ezekiel 7 to the end-times judgment and warns "many of the older commentaries (pre-1900) tend to be non-literal on many of the prophetic promises to Israel." Wiersbe distils the chapter as: "All the things Judah trusted will not help them, not money, idols, or their leaders." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_commentaries; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_71-13)

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik)**: Guzik draws heavily on evangelical scholarship (Block, Taylor, Alexander, Feinberg) and practical application. His emphasis is on God's redemptive purpose in judgment — the goal is always restoration to covenant relationship. No distinctive Pentecostal doctrinal slant on this chapter was evident.

- **Methodist / Wesleyan / Holiness**: No specific Wesleyan commentary on Ezekiel 7 was retrieved from seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu in the searches performed.

- **Lutheran**: No specific Lutheran commentary on Ezekiel 7 was retrieved from lcms.org or 1517.org in the searches performed.

- **Baptist (Spurgeon)**: No Spurgeon-specific material was retrieved for Ezekiel 7.

---

## Other Views

- **Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes / bibleodyssey.org)**: NET Bible notes could not be fetched. Expositor's Bible Commentary (on StudyLight) notes that chapter 7 is "one of those singled out by Ewald as preserving most faithfully the spirit and language of Ezekiel's earlier utterances. Both in thought and expression it exhibits a freedom and animation seldom attained in Ezekiel's writings … The vehemence of his feeling hurries him from one conception to another." The chapter "in some parts unintelligible, and as a whole one of the most difficult in the book." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-7.html)

- **Catholic and Orthodox**: No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on Ezekiel 7 was retrieved from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org in the searches performed.

- **Word of Faith / Prosperity / Hyper-Grace**: No material from these movements on Ezekiel 7 was found in the approved sources.
